articles.headline: Republican Convention.
articles.text:
In accordance with the request of the Republican Territorial Central Committee, we, the undersigned citizens of Billings county, hereby issue this call for a convention to elect a delegate to the Territorial Convention to be held at Huron, April 23, and also to select a Republican County Central Committee. The Billings County Convention to be held at Medora, April 12, 1884, at 2 P. M., at the Hotel de Mores. The attendance of every Republican in the county is earnestly requested.

J. W. Harrison,
Jno. C. Fisher,
Fred Ertel,
T. J. Kerr,
Geo. Blankenberg,
A. T. Packard,
Gill Kennedy,
E. G. Paddock,
G. W. Fitzgerald,
W. F. Houk,
J. W. Reynolds,
Max Bass,
Wm. Van Driesche,
Frank Keeler.
articles.summary: Call, signed by fourteen Billings County citizens including A. T. Packard, for a Republican county convention at the Hotel de Mores, Medora, April 12, 1884.

articles.text: Enough has already been said about the round-up meeting to insure a full attendance, but lest there may be any forgetfulness, we wish to state again that it will be held day after to-morrow at 2 o'clock in the afternoon, in Pennell & Roberts' hall. Let every cattle man attend.
articles.summary: Reminder that the round-up meeting will be held day after to-morrow at 2 p.m. in Pennell & Roberts' hall.

articles.text: Some men, like things "no fellah can find out." The editor of The Mandan Pioneer referred to us as "The handsome and fearless editor of The Bad Lands Cow Boy," and then refused the loan of our cash capital, consisting of eleven cents, two used postage stamps and a shirt and overcoat button, the latter in good condition and almost new. As he scorned our base lucre, it must be that he is working some political scheme. Look out for a dark horse.
articles.summary: Packard jokes that the Mandan Pioneer's editor praised him as handsome and fearless but declined a loan of his eleven-cent capital.

articles.text: The last article in our Dickinson correspondence is a "ringer." The bare truth is sufficient about this country, and in time will bring plenty of men and capital here. We are decidedly not an adherent of the Pat Donan school and think it altogether better to at least mildly insinuate that perhaps there may be a better banana country in the world. In the course of time every lie about this country will be found out and thus "booming" is, to a large extent detrimental. We really believe that we have better natural advantages in the combined production of grain, cattle and coal than any state or territory in the Union. Any one who is cognizant of the fact admits this. Our facilities are rapidly becoming known and they need no exaggeration. Tell the truth and shame Pat D—we mean His Satanic Majesty.
articles.summary: Editorial against exaggerated 'booming' of Dakota in the Pat Donan style, urging the plain truth about the country.

articles.text: In to-day's issue of The Cow Boy we publish a call for a convention to select a delegate to represent this county at the Territorial convention to be held at Huron, the 23d inst., and to select members for a Republican county central committee. Our citizens should turn out at this convention and see that a good man is elected to represent the county at the Territorial convention. We are young yet and prompt and judicious selection will do as much as anything else to bring us to the front. There are many good men here who would well represent the county, but we think the man best fitted in all respects is Mr. Fred Ertel, of Belfield. He is a good business man and will see that the interests of our county do not suffer. As there has been no caucus to decide the matter, we have taken it upon ourselves to fix the date and place for the convention, and have chosen Medora as the most convenient place and April 12 as the day.
articles.summary: Packard urges attendance at the county Republican convention, endorses Fred Ertel of Belfield as delegate to Huron, and explains he set the Medora, April 12 date.

articles.text: The recent riots in Cincinnati are but the outbreak at the sense of wrong every city experiences in the dispensation of justice (?). A cold-blooded, premeditated murder was committed and the jury only sentenced the murderer to imprisonment. A popular outbreak was the result and the bummer element took advantage of this to indulge in wholesele depradations. Justice in cities is getting to be a perfect by-word. One of the most noted criminal lawyers in Chicago told us that if a man had money he would guarantee to free him from any crime. This has also been the case in Cincinnati, and the people determined to put a stop to it and run the shyster lawyers out of town. The result has been that the court house, together with the second-best law library in the United States and many valuable records have been almost totally destroyed. A few more lessons like this and lawyers and juries will learn not to tamper with and pervert justice.
articles.summary: Editorial comment on the Cincinnati courthouse riots as an outbreak against perverted justice.

articles.text:
Telegrams from Miles City state that Deputy Sheriff King and posse have returned from the Upper Rosebud and brought with them thirteen Cheyenne Indians who were participants in the burning of Alderson's ranch. The facts in the case are about as follows: A drunken cow-boy, named Henry Talford, thought it would be extremely funny to shoot a hole through the hat of Black Wolf, a Cheyenne chief. The result was that the Indian received an ugly wound in the head. Returning to his camp Black Wolf's warriors, of course, wanted revenge and started for Alderson's ranch where Talford was working. When the Indians arrived he had skipped the country and no one being at the ranch they vented their rage on the buildings. In connection with these facts it should be known that these Indians have been peaceful, that they were on their reservation and supposed to be supported by the government, when they were nearly starving to death not receiving one-fifth rations, and the attention of the secretary of the interior had to be called to their deplorable condition by the recent meeting of stockmen at Miles City. Also that Black Wolf is one of the best of Indians and that the attack on him was entirely unprovoked.

We must confess that we have no consuming love for Indians, but justice is justice the world over and any infraction we believe should be punished. The Indians knew as well as any of our readers that they would not have obtained justice by recourse to law and they took the only means obtainable to get revenge. Reverse the circumstances and let the unprovoked attack come from an Indian and the matter would never have ended with the burning of a few buildings. Talford tacitly acknowledged his guilt by skipping the country, and he is the man who should have been pursued and brought back for punishment. Because a man is an Indian it does not mean that he has no rights that a white man is bound to respect. Get at the facts in the matter and let punishment fall on the guilty alone.
articles.summary: Report that a Miles City posse brought in thirteen Cheyennes for burning Alderson's ranch, with an editorial arguing the cowboy Henry Talford provoked it by wounding Black Wolf and should be punished.

articles.headline: Dickinson Notes.
articles.text:
Dickinson, March 31, 1884.

Dickinson matters have quieted down since the anxiety about eastern communications has subsided. While the four train loads of passengers were delayed here our streets looked much as we expect to see them when spring business has begun.

A new livery, feed and sale stable is one of the assured additions to the business life of this place.

Mr. Jerry Russell, one of the proprietors of the old stable, is now in the East on a business trip, and is expected soon to return with a car load of horses.

The old coal shed, containing about [1,000?] tons of coal, collapsed Sunday and let several hundred tons of coal fall upon the main track. No damage was caused by the accident.

The resident agent of the Northern Pacific land department has issued a glowing hand-bill setting forth the manifold advantages of this region and calling special attention to the brick yards and freight route, employing a thousand teams, all of which radiates from Dickinson. We should greatly enjoy seeing the realization of these projects, but such references seem a trifle too previous in view of the facts. One trouble, if trouble it be, which embarrasses the boomer class, is the apparently reckless and easy habit of misrepresenting the actual condition of their wares.

The American, and particularly the American of the Great West, is deleriously optimistic; everything is touched with the rose-colored light of his hopeful and imaginative nature. Wherein lies the secret of the great disgust most new settlers feel before they have become mentally, morally and physically acclimated. The simple truth about this country, when it becomes known, will bring men and means to develop it quite as rapidly as consistent with a healthy growth. Do not let us enable some future Dickens to regale the world with a revival of Mark Tapley's Egyptian experience.

Anthropos.
articles.summary: Dickinson correspondence (signed Anthropos): delayed trains, a new livery stable, Jerry Russell's horse-buying trip, collapse of the coal shed, and criticism of the N.P. land agent's booming hand-bill.

articles.headline: Sporting Notes.
articles.text:
A Parker gun club has been organized at Minneapolis.

A cricket club will doubtless be organized in Minneapolis soon.

There will be over 800 entries at the Chicago Driving Park's midsummer meeting.

One hundred and nineteen horses have scored 2:20 or better and twenty-five have beaten 2:17.

Next to the New York dog show the one now open at Toronto is pronounced the best ever held in America.

Whistler and Muldoon wrestled for three hours at San Francisco, the evening of the 20th, neither gaining a fall. It was one of the most exciting contests ever witnessed.

The postponed six-days' go-as-you-please contest will probably commence April 28, at New York. The entries so far are Noremac, Fitzgerald, Vint, Harland and Rowell.

Matsada Sorakichi and Duncan C. Ross will have a wrestling match in Cleveland, April 7. One fall Japanese style, one catch-as-catch-can and the choice of the third will be decided by lot.

Record breaking began early this season. This time it is the hop, skip and jump record, which was raised from 28 feet, 3½ inches to [29?] feet, 2½ inches by M. W. Ford, at a meeting of the New York atheletic club last week.

The Baltimore Union Club intends to have band music before games and between innings this season. It is an unmitigated nuisance and we will guarantee that the players will have the band fired before the first week's play is ended.

From the make-up of the clubs it now looks as though Minneapolis would win the Northwestern league championship; the Chicago's that of the league; the Athletics that of the American league, and the Chicago Unions that of the Union league. St. Paul seems destined for a place near the foot of the Northwestern League.

The Milwaukee management has decided not to play Sunday games of base-ball and thereto the Grand Rapids Democrat howls its violent opposition. We heartily concur with the Milwaukee management in their decision. Base-ball is just rising to the position it should rightfully occupy—the king of American sports. As long as Sunday games are allowed, so long will its old reputation cling to it. In the past, it has been a gamblers' game. Owing to the efforts of Mr. Hulbert in doing away with Sunday games, it received its first lift toward respectability, and now we are surprised to see a paper supporting a measure that will inevitably lower the standard of base-ball. If for no other reason than as a day of rest, ball-players should not play on Sundays. They are worked hard enough during the week.

The prize fight between Sullivan and Thompson now seems to be an assured fact. It will be fought according to the rules of the London prize ring in either Louisiana, Texas or Kansas, with or without gloves at Sullivan's option. The forfeit is deposited, articles signed and the fight will be for $5,000 a side and the championship of the world. Only six persons on a side will be allowed as witnesses.
articles.summary: Packard's column of national sporting news, with his comment against band music and Sunday base-ball.

articles.headline: On the Range. Call for Bad Lands Association.
articles.text:
There will be a meeting held at Little Missouri crossing, the third Monday in April (the 21st) for the purpose of forming a Bad Lands Association. All raisers of live stock are requested to attend. Upon its organization, business of much importance will come before the association and it is to the interest of every man interested in live stock to attend.

The Committee.
articles.summary: Call for a meeting at Little Missouri crossing on Monday, April 21, to form a Bad Lands stockmen's association.

articles.headline: Notice—Round-Up.
articles.text: All Bad Lands cattle men and those having any interest in a Bad Lands round-up are requested to meet here on the morning of April 5, to arrange for an annual round-up of this region.
articles.summary: Notice asking Bad Lands cattlemen to meet April 5 to arrange an annual round-up.

articles.text: A hog raiser in this county, four years ago started with two sows. During that time he has sold $400 of hogs and his stock now on hand is worth $350; all from two sows.—[Minneapolis Messenger.
articles.summary: Reprint: a Minnesota hog raiser's profits from two sows.

articles.text: Eastern Montana stockmen have wisely decided to take all bulls from the herds on the 1st of November and keep them separated therefrom until the 1st of July of each year.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprint: Eastern Montana stockmen to separate bulls from herds November to July.

articles.text: Stockmen continue to arrive daily in this city from the ranges, and all report that the cattle and stock generally are in splendid condition. They are predicting an unprecedented influx of stockmen into this section of the country this spring and summer, and one and all claim this country to be without a peer.—[Yellowstone, Mont., Journal.
articles.summary: Reprint: Yellowstone Journal reports stock in splendid condition and a coming influx of stockmen.

articles.text: Montana beeves have stood as high or higher than those of any other grazing region, owing in part to the presence of good blood; but this large introduction of blooded animals into the herds south will be likely to change this and place Montana beef in the background, unless our herds are improved by the same process.—[Helena, Mont., Independent.
articles.summary: Reprint: Montana beef may lose its standing unless herds are improved with blooded stock.

articles.text: Two or three hundred new cattle ranches will not overstock the bunch grass ranges of the Bad Lands and Montana but from the number of cattle companies and individuals getting ready to take stock in this spring, we doubt whether there will be much vacant grazing territory left next spring. People who think of going into this safe and profitable business should be up and doing.—[Northwest.
articles.summary: Reprint: so many cattle outfits are entering the Bad Lands and Montana that little vacant range may remain by next spring.

articles.text: Cattlemen of the northwest must be active and positive in their policy to prevent the introduction of infectious diseases into their herds. They must provide unquestioned security and leave no act undone for the good of the industry. Great care and sound discretion must guide every step. There should be no mistakes in a matter that involves the wealth of half a dozen states and territories.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprint: northwestern cattlemen urged to guard herds against infectious disease.

articles.text: There are thirteen crooks lingering behind the bars of the Bent county jail, all of whom can trace the cause of their arrest to the effective work of a successful stock growers' association. With stockmen, forbearance has ceased to be a virtue and "iron bars" will be brought into requisition in other counties before the season of 1884 is over, unless the "stray stock pullers" take a timely warning.—[Hurricane, Colo., Cactus.
articles.summary: Reprint: a Colorado stock growers' association has put thirteen rustlers in the Bent county jail.

articles.text: Windgalls are produced by sprains of the tendons and these may occur in many ways. The treatment of the puffy swellings consists in reducing the inflammation by cold applications, as pounded ice or a solution of saltpetre and salt in cold water, and then favoring absorption by blistering. Rest is necessary during the treatment. Sometimes the blister may need repeating two or three times, but always after a sufficient interval to permit the effects to pass off. After every effort the trouble will return whenever excessive strain is brought upon the weakened tendon.—[Kansas City Live Stock Indicator.
articles.summary: Reprint: treatment of windgalls in horses.

articles.text: There is a wide difference of opinion among Texas men who claim opportunities for making an estimate as to the number of cattle likely to take the trail for the north the coming spring. The highest estimates we have heard, place the number at 350,000, while the lowest is 150,000. From all the information we have been able to gather it is doubtful, in our opinion, if the drive amounts to more than a quarter of a million head, and even this, we think, is a very liberal estimate. Double that number of Texas cattle will change hands but about half of them will be sold in connection with Texas ranges, or to ranchmen owning herds on neighboring ranges.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprint: estimates of the coming Texas trail drive north range from 150,000 to 350,000 head.

articles.text:
We hail with pleasure the birth of a new Dakota paper, The Bad Lands Cow Boy. Its proprietor and editor is the Marquis de Mores, son of the Duc de Vallombrosa, who is well known in France as the leader of the social world at Cannes. The Cow Boy is really a neat little journal, with lots to read in it, and the American press has every reason to be proud of its new baby. We are quite sure it will live to be a credit to its family. The Cow Boy evidently means business. It says in the introductory notice in its first number that it intends to be the leading cattle paper of the Northwest and adds that it is not published for fun but for two dollars a year.—New York Herald.

No comments; no cards.
articles.summary: Reprinted New York Herald notice welcoming the Cow Boy and wrongly naming the Marquis de Morès as its proprietor and editor; Packard adds only 'No comments; no cards.'

articles.headline: The Beef Traffic.
articles.text:
It is now quite certain that Marquis de Mores, who has engaged very extensively in the beef trade at Medora, will create a branch business at Deadwood just as soon as a railroad from any point reaches us. He has taken a contract to furnish New York with forty cars of dressed beef, and to do this kills 200 head each day. He buys large numbers from Wyoming and all sections, taking them to Medora. The dressed meat is placed in refrigerator cars and shipped through to that city in as fresh a condition as when first slaughtered. He has indicated his intention to establish a branch at this place just as soon as he can be afforded steam transportation.

It is needless to comment upon the impetus, such an industry would lend to the business of the Hills, but alone is of sufficient importance to elicit every effort of our people to encourage the completion of a road to this point. It would make a steady market for the fatted cattle of this section and throw large sums of money into circulation here that now is captured by other places so far distant from us that its stimulating effects are not experienced by our people. Such an enterprise, aside from the financial benefits, will afford ample employment for a large number of men, and would form one more substantial and lasting feature to the Hills.—[Minnesela Boomer.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Minnesela (Dakota) Boomer: the Marquis de Morès, killing 200 head a day at Medora on a 40-car New York contract, plans a Black Hills branch once a railroad arrives.

articles.headline: Improve the Stock.
articles.text:
I have yet to find any stock raiser dissatisfied with his efforts to improve his stock, provided he has given care and attention to his business. Of course, there are plenty of men in Texas, as elsewhere, who carelessly start into any business and neglect it, that grumble at their want of success. Some of these cry down blooded stock. Let us briefly consider the question of which pays the best to keep, a blooded bull or a Spanish scrub? Take the Spanish bull, turn him out to rustle for himself; spring finds him poor and weak, when he is old enough for service, his fight with poverty has left him a poor subject to breed from, if he gets one-half the calves of cows served he will have done remarkably well, and these calves are generally thriftless little fellows that develop into small beeves at maturity and sell at low figures. Take the blooded bull, pasture and care for him until he reaches the proper age for duty. Expend cotton seed, corn, oats and millet upon him. When he is put to service the result is ninety per cent of good strong calves that will mature a year younger and weigh full 300 pounds more than our Spanish bull's produce, and sell for at least $15 a head more in market. Say the Spanish bull gets 25 out of 50 cows, and these calves at four years old sell for $25 a head or $625. The shorthorn gets 45 calves, which at three years old sell for $40 per head or $1,800. Now the loss from the failure to produce of the 25 cows bred to the Spanish bull, will amply cover all the expense of feed and extra keep of the blooded bull. A merchant's rule is to handle the goods that is the quickest sale and bring the best returns. Stockmen should follow suit.

The above illustration I know to be true for I have seen them sell together on the market. Three years ago I was at the Stock Yards at Chicago and had some very good native steers (Missouri cattle) for which I obtained $4.75 per hundred, thinking I had made a pretty good sale. Mr. Hall, of Hall, Greer & Co., called my attention to a car-load of Colorado half-breed Herefords in a pen opposite my stock that a purchaser was just closing the trade for at $5 per hundred. I asked, "How does it come that those range cattle bring more money than my natives?"

"Well," said he, "I will explain it to you. Those cattle are no better than yours as far as flesh is concerned, but in the long run makes the shrinkage heavier and they kill better than your cattle for they come such a long distance there isn't anything but beef in them when they get here, and being wild and unaccustomed to being penned they won't eat or drink to do any good, while your cattle are quiet and gentle, will eat all they want and take a big fill of water, etc., making [quite a difference?], you see."

Then he said: "Now, I have just given you a minor reason; here is a load of cattle off of the same ranch, but are nothing but scrubs. I only sold them for $4.25 per hundred, and they are just as good in flesh as those over there, but don't you see these half-breeds are of a uniform color. All look very nearly alike!"

There is the beauty of breeding blooded stock. If you get a bull that has been bred a solid color, he will make seven calves out of ten just like him. I think that load of cattle the finest I have ever seen. They had been sorted out and put in a load to themselves, and they well paid the owner for his trouble, for the buyers were two to one for that load of cattle to any other in the yard. They had been shipped from Colorado to Nebraska and corned about three months, and they were perfect beauties. These were not all the grade cattle I've seen knock the socks off of scrubs. I have seen numbers of them. I followed shipping to Chicago for three years and it very often came under my notice. You can ship two loads of cattle to St. Louis any day, one of the Spanish and the other half-breeds, and your half-breeds will bring from twenty-five to fifty cents per hundred over your scrubs every time.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Texas Live Stock Journal arguing that blooded bulls pay better than Spanish scrubs.

articles.text: Union base-ball umpires receive $140 per month and all expenses.
articles.summary: Note on Union league umpires' pay.

articles.text: Ready-print inside page (with a 'Bad Lands Cow Boy, A. T. Packard, publisher' header) carrying 'The Pith of the News' national and foreign wire news, crimes and casualties, Dakota News Notes, the official call for the Dakota Republican territorial convention at Huron, a congressional summary, and wit and humor.
articles.summary: Ready-print national, foreign and territorial news page; not transcribed (one item about the Cow Boy is transcribed separately).

articles.text: "The Bad Lands Cowboy," is the unique title of a thorough cattle paper, published at Medora, Dak., which is fast becoming a noted cattle point. It gives all the cattle and general news of the Bad lands, and advocates Medora as the cattle headquarters of the Northwest. The name of the paper calls attention to the two things concerning which the editor, A. T. Packard, wishes to change public opinion, as the Bad Lands are not bad, but very good, and produce mints of money; and the cow-boys, as a rule, are good citizens. The exceptions have formed public opinion against them.
articles.summary: Item in the ready-print 'Dakota News Notes' column describing the Cow Boy and its editor A. T. Packard.

articles.text: Ready-print page: fiction and essays ('Our Old-Fashioned Parties', 'For Charlie's Sake'), miscellany and reminiscences, and patent-medicine and mail-order advertising (Cuticura, Allen's Lung Balsam, Hostetter's Bitters, Tutt's Pills, Saskatchewan Fife Wheat, Frazer Axle Grease and others).
articles.summary: Ready-print fiction, miscellany and patent-medicine advertising; not transcribed.

articles.text: A trial of the Far West cigar is its best recommendation.
articles.summary: Reading notice for the Far West cigar.

articles.text: Mr. J. C. Beekman Fish, a New York banker and broker, is visiting the Marquis.
articles.summary: New York banker J. C. Beekman Fish is visiting the Marquis de Morès.

articles.text: Mr. Geo. Roderick has claimed the butte north of town and is now "holding it down."
articles.summary: George Roderick has claimed the butte north of town.

articles.text: A. J. Monroe, of Junction City, an old friend of Frank Keeler, is in town for a few days.
articles.summary: A. J. Monroe of Junction City, a friend of Frank Keeler, is visiting.

articles.summary: F. B. Allen, secretary of the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., is expected shortly.

articles.text: There were two sections of No. 1 this morning, both very heavy trains. The first section had eleven coaches.
articles.summary: Westbound No. 1 ran in two heavy sections this morning.

articles.text: Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, have given Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.
articles.summary: Roberts & Co. get the sole Little Missouri agency for the Far West cigar from Wise & Goodkind of Bismarck.

articles.text: Now that spring is fairly upon us, the cleaning up season commences. Every one who can rustle a rake is hard at work.
articles.summary: Spring cleaning-up season has begun in town.

articles.text: The company's hides were all packed and shipped Saturday. Such a favorable impression was made on both sides that Mr. Hample will doubtless be the future buyer here.
articles.summary: The company's hides were shipped Saturday, and Mr. Hample is likely to be the future buyer.

articles.text: A visit to the store of Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, is rather an eye-opener on the way business is done in the West. They carry a stock that would do credit to any city firm.
articles.summary: Praise for the Bismarck store of Wise & Goodkind.

articles.text: The gang of men who are putting up the through telegraph wire between St. Paul and Portland arrived here yesterday. They are making from twelve to twenty miles a day.
articles.summary: The crew stringing the through St. Paul-Portland telegraph wire reached town yesterday.

articles.text: M. J. Mahon, of Mandan, is on deck this week with an advertisement of his restaurant. From personal experience we can assert that he gives perfect satisfaction. Mike's is certainly the place to make your "Headquarters" while in Mandan.
articles.summary: Notice of M. J. Mahon's new advertisement for his Mandan restaurant.

articles.text: Mr. John Nye, a Livingstone and Deadwood capitalist, was in town Tuesday and thinks strongly of interesting himself in the Medora freight route. He has formerly been a forwarding agent and understands the freight business thoroughly.
articles.summary: Capitalist John Nye visited Tuesday and is considering investing in the Medora freight route.

articles.text: M. G. Hall, assistant superintendent of the Northern Pacific Express Co., came in this morning on the second section of No. 1. He expects to make Medora an express station very soon, which will be a great convenience to the citizens on this side of the river.
articles.summary: M. G. Hall of the Northern Pacific Express Co. arrived and plans to make Medora an express station.

articles.text: A visit to the furniture rooms of Duncan & Hillis, in Mandan, disclosed the fact that for the future there will be no more going to St. Paul to buy. Their stock compares favorably with that carried by any city firm, and one who cannot be suited there is certainly hard to please.
articles.summary: Praise for the Duncan & Hillis furniture rooms in Mandan.

articles.text: Mr. M. L. Kramer, of Pueblo, Colo., has been in town for several days to attend the round-up meeting, to be held next Saturday. He owns about 15,000 head of cattle in Colorado and will perhaps drive up a number of beeves to fatten in the Bad Lands. He is much pleased with the country.
articles.summary: Colorado cattleman M. L. Kramer is in town for the round-up meeting and may drive beeves to the Bad Lands.

articles.text: Mr. Flynn, of Mandan, is intending to start a boot and shoe store here. As yet he is undecided whether he will give it his personal attention or make it a branch store. In either event it will be a needed addition. Mr. Flynn is well known throughout this whole country and has hosts of friends who will patronize him.
articles.summary: Mr. Flynn of Mandan plans a boot and shoe store in town.

articles.text: It has just been learned that Mr. Matthias, the superintendent of this, the Missouri division, has resigned to take effect in a few days. The cause of his action is unknown, but we will certainly be sorry to see him go. No word can be said against his management and in private he is one of the most courteous gentleman we have ever met.
articles.summary: Mr. Matthias, N. P. superintendent of the Missouri division, has resigned.

articles.text: Could our subscribers read some of our letters from the East it would surprise them to know the general interest and in a good many cases the ignorance of eastern persons in reference to the Bad Lands. In nearly every letter some reference is made to intended visits and all express a decided curiosity to see the wonders of the Bad Lands. The number of last year's sight-seers will be doubled this summer. The most of these are persons of capital and many will be induced to stay.
articles.summary: Letters from the East show growing interest in visiting the Bad Lands; sight-seers expected to double this summer.

articles.text: A visit to Mandan and Bismarck has disclosed to us the fact that every one there is interested in Medora. Eleven lots have been spoken for in those two places, and they will doubtless go off like hot cakes. First come, first served is the rule, and our citizens should see to it that all the choice lots are not gobbled by outsiders. We have only space to say to-day that the deeds arrived this morning and prices may be learned by a visit to The Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Eleven Medora lots have been spoken for in Mandan and Bismarck; the deeds arrived this morning and prices are available at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: Some crank at Dickinson has issued a luminous circular advertising the town and speaks in glowing terms of the thousand teams on the Dickinson freight route. We wonder if said crank has ever thought of the result of one of these circulars falling into the hands of an intending settler there and the sense of disgust he will have when he finds out the bare-faced lie. For the sake of Dickinson and this whole country, such a nuisance as this agent has proved himself to be should be abated. Will the sensible citizens of Dickinson cork him up?
articles.summary: Attack on a Dickinson circular claiming a thousand teams on the Dickinson freight route.

articles.text: Smoke the Far West cigar, sold only by Roberts & Co.
articles.summary: Reading notice for the Far West cigar at Roberts & Co.

articles.text: A new barber has taken the place of the bold soldier boy who has gone back to the defence of his country.
articles.summary: A new barber has replaced the soldier who returned to the army.

articles.text: Mr. Sam English, well known to many of our citizens, is on his way to Medora to engage in business. He will be a welcome addition.
articles.summary: Sam English is coming to Medora to go into business.

articles.text: We are anxious to hear from "How" again, and if he doesn't show-up soon we will give him away and let the wrath of the community down on his devoted head.
articles.summary: Packard teases an anonymous contributor signing himself 'How'.

articles.text: The smiling countenance of "Big Foot" Ryder has been beaming on our citizens for a day or two. "The gang" is resting from its arduous labors until the June freshet.
articles.summary: 'Big Foot' Ryder is in town; his gang is idle until the June freshet.

articles.text: Again has Frank Smith placed our Bad Lands museum under obligations to him. One specimen has the plain print of water flags upon it, although it was found on the top of a high butte.
articles.summary: Frank Smith gave the Bad Lands museum a fossil specimen with water-flag prints found on a high butte.

articles.text: The immigration edition of The Mandan Pioneer has had the good effect of influencing several persons to write us in reference to the Bad Lands. From recent letters we are convinced that one at least will settle here.
articles.summary: The Mandan Pioneer's immigration edition has prompted inquiries about settling in the Bad Lands.

articles.text: The following is an extract from a letter written in Paris, France, to a friend of ours in Medora: "The Bad Lands Cow Boy is a favorite of mine. Be sure and send it to me regularly. Give my kindest regards to the editor and wish him every success." She is the right kind to stick to, William.
articles.summary: Extract from a Paris letter to a Medora man praising the Cow Boy.

articles.text: The knight of the curry-comb tackled a cotton pie April 1, and in his herculean efforts to swallow it and not give the thing away to his fellow boarders, his eyes rolled out on the bridge of his nose until they gazed into each others countenances, and the boys never "smiled," oh, no!
articles.summary: April Fool's prank: a stableman was served a cotton pie on April 1.

articles.text: One of the strangest displays of aurora borealis it has ever been our lot to witness was seen last Friday night. The usual flickerings were greatly magnified, but the climax was reached with a broad band of light looking exactly like a dense mist extending across the heavens from the eastern to the western horizon. The greatest display of lights was also from the eastern horizon.
articles.summary: An unusual aurora borealis was seen last Friday night.

articles.text: Messrs. Hyde and Wilkes left Tuesday night for Chicago to visit their families for a week or two. Mr. Hyde will bring his family back with him and live at the Cantonment until his residence is completed. Mr. Wilkes, though strongly urged by a number of would-be sons-in-law, could not be prevailed upon to bring his family back with him. Oh, George, how could you be so cruel?
articles.summary: Hyde and Wilkes left Tuesday night for Chicago; Hyde will bring his family back to live at the Cantonment.

articles.text: The stockmen's ball Saturday night bids fair to eclipse anything of the kind held in Little Missouri. Every preparation has been made. First-class music from Glendive will be in attendance and supper will be served at a convenient hour. The best of order is guaranteed and everything will doubtless pass off pleasantly. Messrs. Keeler and Goodall are well known enough to insure this. Tickets, including supper, are only $2.50 each, and no one can afford to miss the good time.
articles.summary: A stockmen's ball, with Glendive music and supper, is planned for Saturday night under Keeler and Goodall.

articles.text: We received a call from Mr. Gregor Lang last week, and he reports that his cattle are in prime condition. Only a few head have died, and as a jelly-like substance was found about the joints of each one, there is no doubt that the deaths were due to the bruises the cattle received in the railroad accident. Mr. Lang has a first-rate ranch about fifty miles up the river and will put a thousand more cattle on it this spring. He will soon begin to erect a brick house and when completed will bring out his family.
articles.summary: Gregor Lang reports his cattle in prime condition, plans to add a thousand head and build a brick house on his ranch fifty miles up the river.

articles.text: It will be a matter of interest and news to the most of our readers that a new road has been found out of the Bad Lands to the divide, for our freight route. It is even better than the old one and at least five miles shorter, the distance to the divide being now eighteen miles or less. There was no serious need of bridges, but five have been put in so that the road in the Bad Lands is now almost as good as that on the divide. Very little grading was required. A gang of men under Joe Pennell have been at work for several days and by to-night or to-morrow, at farthest, our route will be finished and be then the most perfect one that there has ever been or will be west of the Missouri. Considerable additional freight has come and a trip will soon be made. A large number of additional contracts have been made by Mr. Jones, at Deadwood, guaranteeing an abundance of freighting for the whole 400 teams that will start from Medora.
articles.summary: A new, shorter freight road from the Bad Lands to the divide, with five bridges built by Joe Pennell's crew, is nearly finished; 400 teams are to start from Medora.

articles.text: The Marquis and Mr. Sleeper returned early this morning. They came in on the first through train that has run from Bismarck for nearly a week. The old track has been washed away for two miles and a temporary track was laid on the prairie. Mr. Sleeper, on being "held up," stated that every thing in regard to the company's business is working in the most satisfactory manner. An abundance of ice has been put up at all the places where cold-storage houses have been or are now being erected. Most of the cold-storage houses are near completion and will be ready for business as soon as the summer killing begins. Large contracts have been made in New York for dressed beef and this trade alone will keep the abattoirs busy. The retail merchants up and down the line have already signified their intention of purchasing almost wholly from the company's cold-storage houses and a prosperous business season will open almost immediately. In addition to the buildings now being erected, it was found necessary to add one to the already large St. Paul facilities of the company. The Marquis intends going on to Helena almost immediately and Mr. Sleeper will return to St. Paul.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès and C. W. Sleeper returned this morning on the first through train from Bismarck in nearly a week; Sleeper reports ice stored, cold-storage houses nearly done and big New York beef contracts.

articles.headline: For Rent.
articles.text:
For Rent.

The frame building south of the Cow Boy office. For terms, apply to A. T. Packard.
articles.summary: Packard offers the frame building south of the Cow Boy office for rent.

articles.text: The boys always manage to enjoy themselves here, but a little the most uproarious time we have had lately was at the expense of Mr. Hample, who has lately bought the company's hides. It seems that when Mr. Hample cannot get hide quotations he makes his rates from the other market reports, especially on wheat and corn. Last Friday evening Mr. Fisher became apparently very much interested in reading a paper, and finally laid it down with the remark that the market seemed wonderfully depressed. Mr. Hample became deeply interested at once, and taking up the paper turned eagerly to the market reports. Wheat, 52c; corn, 27c, was the first thing he saw and his hair began to raise like the fur of an angry Sir Thomas cat. By comparison, the hides that he had just bought and made a first payment of $10,000 on, were worth but little if any more than the $10,000. Vain efforts were made by him to buy off from his contract. A more thoroughly "broke up" man we have never seen until a kind friend showed him the date of the paper—March 23, 1840.
articles.summary: Joke played last Friday evening on hide buyer Mr. Hample with an 1840 newspaper's market reports.

articles.text: The Far West is the best cigar in the city. The Senate holds the sole agency.
articles.summary: Reading notice: the Senate holds the Far West cigar agency.

articles.text:
At last we have found some one who realizes the money there is in such a venture and a brick-yard and pottery works will soon be in active operation here. Mr. Peter Book, of Mandan, is the gentleman to whom we refer. He is one of the best known masons and contract- there, that he built the People's block being a sufficient recommendation. Mr. Book will be here next week, as he is only waiting in Mandan to close up his business. The clay with which our buttes abound he says will make brick of a beautiful dark red color, exactly similar to the famous St. Louis brick. It is also the very best quality of pottery clay, and as Mr. Book has had long experience in making both brick and pottery he has every hope of being completely successful in their manufacture here. He also expects to make pressed brick exclusively, as aside from the cost of the presses they can be made as cheaply and will command a far readier sale. There will be a splendid market for both the brick and pottery, and Mr. Book is to be congratulated on his foresight in entering into the business at this point.

Smoke the Far West.
articles.summary: Mason Peter Book of Mandan will open a brick-yard and pottery works at Medora, arriving next week.

events.summary: Fourteen Billings County citizens, A. T. Packard among them, called a county Republican convention for April 12 at the Hotel de Mores in Medora to choose a delegate to the Huron territorial convention and a county central committee.
events.excerpt: The Billings County Convention to be held at Medora, April 12, 1884, at 2 P. M., at the Hotel de Mores.

events.excerpt: we think the man best fitted in all respects is Mr. Fred Ertel, of Belfield.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday night" before Thu 3 Apr 1884
events.title: Hyde and Wilkes leave for Chicago
events.summary: Messrs. Hyde and Wilkes left for Chicago to visit their families; Hyde planned to bring his family back to live at the Cantonment until his house was finished.
events.excerpt: Messrs. Hyde and Wilkes left Tuesday night for Chicago to visit their families for a week or two.

events.date_basis: "Saturday night" after Thu 3 Apr 1884
events.title: Stockmen's ball planned
events.summary: A stockmen's ball managed by Keeler and Goodall was planned for Saturday night, with music from Glendive and supper; tickets $2.50.
events.excerpt: The stockmen's ball Saturday night bids fair to eclipse anything of the kind held in Little Missouri.

events.date_basis: "last week" before Thu 3 Apr 1884
events.title: Gregor Lang reports his cattle in prime condition
events.summary: Gregor Lang called at the paper and said his cattle were in prime condition, with a few deaths from injuries in the railroad accident; he planned to add a thousand head this spring and build a brick house on his ranch about fifty miles up the river.
events.excerpt: Mr. Lang has a first-rate ranch about fifty miles up the river and will put a thousand more cattle on it this spring.

events.date_basis: "by to-night or to-morrow" from Thu 3 Apr 1884
events.title: New Medora freight road to the divide nearly finished
events.summary: A new road out of the Bad Lands to the divide for the Medora freight route, at least five miles shorter, with five bridges built by Joe Pennell's crew, was to be finished that night or the next day; Mr. Jones at Deadwood had made contracts for freight for 400 teams.
events.excerpt: A gang of men under Joe Pennell have been at work for several days and by to-night or to-morrow, at farthest, our route will be finished

events.date_basis: "early this morning" Thu 3 Apr 1884
events.title: Marquis de Morès and Sleeper return on first through train in a week
events.summary: The Marquis de Morès and C. W. Sleeper returned on the first through train from Bismarck in nearly a week, after two miles of track washed out; Sleeper said ice was stored and the cold-storage houses were nearly finished, and the Marquis was going on to Helena.
events.excerpt: They came in on the first through train that has run from Bismarck for nearly a week.

events.date_basis: Washout lasted "nearly a week" before Thu 3 Apr 1884
events.title: Washout halts through trains from Bismarck
events.summary: Two miles of Northern Pacific track had been washed away, and no through train ran from Bismarck for nearly a week until a temporary track was laid on the prairie.
events.excerpt: The old track has been washed away for two miles and a temporary track was laid on the prairie.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 3 Apr 1884 issue
events.title: Brick-yard and pottery works coming to Medora
events.summary: Peter Book, a Mandan mason and contractor, planned to open a brick-yard and pottery works using butte clay, arriving the next week.
events.excerpt: Mr. Peter Book, of Mandan, is the gentleman to whom we refer.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 3 Apr 1884 issue
events.title: Roberts & Co. get Far West cigar agency
events.summary: Wise & Goodkind of Bismarck gave Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.
events.excerpt: Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, have given Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 3 Apr 1884 issue
events.title: Eastern letters show rising interest in Bad Lands visits
events.summary: The paper said letters from the East showed curiosity about the Bad Lands and predicted last year's sight-seers would double this summer.
events.excerpt: The number of last year's sight-seers will be doubled this summer.
